title: Comparing curved and straight outlines in a room sketch
description: Curved and straight outlines can be compared without deciding the final object.

sections.heading: The question behind the worksheet
paragraphs: Curved and straight outlines can be compared without deciding the final object. The useful question is how each outline relates to the room and its existing forms.

sections.heading: Work through the observation
paragraphs: Trace two alternatives at the same stated scale or clearly label them approximate. Place each in the same room sketch. Compare visible mass, edge relationships and movement questions separately. Keep colour out of the first comparison if it distracts from the outline.

sections.heading: A worked example to compare
paragraphs: A curved outline may soften the visual relationship to a rectangular rug, while a straight edge may align with nearby cabinetry. Those are different intentions, not universal advantages.

sections.heading: Questions to put in your notes
paragraphs: Use these prompts to produce a short record you can revisit. Date the sheet, identify the reference you used and leave unknowns explicitly unanswered. Keep site facts, personal preferences and requests for confirmation separate.
checklist: Which relationship changes with the curve?

sections.heading: What this exercise cannot establish
paragraphs: An outline study does not establish edge safety, usable dimensions or construction feasibility. Those require a later specification.

title: How negative space affects an object arrangement
description: Empty space is part of an arrangement because it affects how objects are read together.

sections.heading: The question behind the worksheet
paragraphs: Empty space is part of an arrangement because it affects how objects are read together. It should be described intentionally rather than treated as whatever remains after placement.

sections.heading: Work through the observation
paragraphs: Draw the main objects as simple filled shapes. Look at the gaps between them and around the whole group. Compare a tighter and a looser arrangement using the same objects. Note whether each reads as one group or several independent elements.

sections.heading: A worked example to compare
paragraphs: Two objects placed close together may read as a pair. Moving one farther away can make both feel separate even though neither object changes.

sections.heading: Questions to put in your notes
paragraphs: Use these prompts to produce a short record you can revisit. Date the sheet, identify the reference you used and leave unknowns explicitly unanswered. Keep site facts, personal preferences and requests for confirmation separate.
checklist: What space is needed for use?

sections.heading: What this exercise cannot establish
paragraphs: Visual spacing is not a substitute for safe access or mounting advice. Real dimensions and use must be considered before an arrangement is fixed.

title: Planning a pair with different heights
description: A pair with different heights can create a relationship without looking identical.

sections.heading: The question behind the worksheet
paragraphs: A pair with different heights can create a relationship without looking identical. Start by deciding whether the pair should act together or serve different positions.

sections.heading: Work through the observation
paragraphs: Sketch the two profiles side by side and from the usual viewing angle. Mark the proposed shared feature, such as a colour direction or edge rhythm. Describe how each is intended to be used. Compare overlap in the drawing without assuming the pieces can nest or stack.

sections.heading: A worked example to compare
paragraphs: A taller form behind a lower one might create depth in a composition. That drawing alone does not mean their bases, stability or surfaces are compatible.

sections.heading: Questions to put in your notes
paragraphs: Use these prompts to produce a short record you can revisit. Date the sheet, identify the reference you used and leave unknowns explicitly unanswered. Keep site facts, personal preferences and requests for confirmation separate.

sections.heading: What this exercise cannot establish
paragraphs: Nesting, stacking and loading are functional claims requiring confirmation. Keep a visual pairing separate from those claims.

title: Using repetition without identical objects
description: Repetition can come from a shared detail rather than exact copies.

sections.heading: The question behind the worksheet
paragraphs: Repetition can come from a shared detail rather than exact copies. A brief becomes more flexible when it identifies what repeats and what may vary.

sections.heading: Work through the observation
paragraphs: Choose one recurring element: an outline, a tonal relationship or a spacing rhythm. Make a small comparison sheet showing variations around that element. Label intentional differences. Review the group from a distance as well as each item separately.

sections.heading: A worked example to compare
paragraphs: A set might repeat a blue accent while allowing each grain-like pattern to differ. The recurring colour direction provides continuity without promising identical visual marks.

sections.heading: Questions to put in your notes
paragraphs: Use these prompts to produce a short record you can revisit. Date the sheet, identify the reference you used and leave unknowns explicitly unanswered. Keep site facts, personal preferences and requests for confirmation separate.
checklist: How will the group be recognised without identical details?

sections.heading: What this exercise cannot establish
paragraphs: Natural-looking variation in an illustration does not establish how real materials will vary. The final method and acceptable variation need discussion.

title: Framing the view around a wall piece
description: The wall around a piece influences its composition.

sections.heading: The question behind the worksheet
paragraphs: The wall around a piece influences its composition. A reference cropped tightly to the artwork cannot explain its relationship to nearby openings, furniture or light.

sections.heading: Work through the observation
paragraphs: Photograph the wall broadly, then mark the proposed viewing area on a copy. Add the outline of nearby furniture and openings. Compare the composition from the entrance and a usual seated position. Keep mounting questions on a separate list.

sections.heading: A worked example to compare
paragraphs: A frame may appear centred on the wall but off-centre relative to a console beneath it. Decide which relationship matters before requesting a final position.

sections.heading: Questions to put in your notes
paragraphs: Use these prompts to produce a short record you can revisit. Date the sheet, identify the reference you used and leave unknowns explicitly unanswered. Keep site facts, personal preferences and requests for confirmation separate.
checklist: What is the visual reference line?
Which surrounding element anchors the composition?

paragraphs: A composition sketch does not confirm a wall's mounting suitability, fixing method or load capacity. Those need specific assessment.

title: Recording three doorway views of the same console position
description: Three doorway views can reveal a console position that looks balanced only from one angle.

sections.heading: The question behind the worksheet
paragraphs: Three doorway views can reveal a console position that looks balanced only from one angle. The comparison is most useful when the images are taken under similar conditions.

sections.heading: Work through the observation
paragraphs: Photograph from the threshold, one step to the left and one step to the right where safe. Keep the proposed position marked consistently. Note what disappears behind the door, furniture or wall return. Compare the whole silhouette before concentrating on details.

sections.heading: A worked example to compare
paragraphs: A waterfall-like end may be prominent from one side and almost invisible from the other. The brief can then explain which approach view matters most.

sections.heading: Questions to put in your notes
paragraphs: Use these prompts to produce a short record you can revisit. Date the sheet, identify the reference you used and leave unknowns explicitly unanswered. Keep site facts, personal preferences and requests for confirmation separate.
checklist: Which part remains visible in every view?
What does the preferred photograph conceal?

sections.heading: What this exercise cannot establish
paragraphs: Different viewpoints do not prove the reference image depicts an actual room or installed piece. Label concept imagery and site photographs separately.

title: Balancing a low object with nearby seating
description: A low object's relationship to seating is both visual and practical.

sections.heading: The question behind the worksheet
paragraphs: A low object's relationship to seating is both visual and practical. Begin with the seating that will actually remain in the room rather than a generic styled reference.

sections.heading: Work through the observation
paragraphs: Draw the object and nearby seats in plan and side view. Record the intended activity and the main viewing position. Separate preferred proportions from measured seating dimensions. Ask about practical use before treating a visual alignment as a specification.

sections.heading: A worked example to compare
paragraphs: A low round form might look quiet between two chairs, but the drawing must still explain how people approach and use the area. Appearance alone cannot answer that.

sections.heading: Questions to put in your notes
paragraphs: Use these prompts to produce a short record you can revisit. Date the sheet, identify the reference you used and leave unknowns explicitly unanswered. Keep site facts, personal preferences and requests for confirmation separate.
checklist: What must be checked beyond appearance?

paragraphs: Do not infer comfortable reach, stability or suitability from a room scene. The real users and confirmed dimensions need review.

title: Considering a sculptural object from several viewpoints
description: A sculptural object may change substantially as the viewer moves.

sections.heading: The question behind the worksheet
paragraphs: A sculptural object may change substantially as the viewer moves. A single front view can therefore give an incomplete brief.

sections.heading: Work through the observation
paragraphs: Choose a primary view and two secondary views. Describe the silhouette, visible openings and apparent depth in each. Note whether the object is intended to be seen from all sides or against a wall. Keep observations about the image separate from proposed changes.

sections.heading: A worked example to compare
paragraphs: A clear block can appear dense from one angle and open from another because the contents overlap differently. That change may be part of the visual interest.

sections.heading: Questions to put in your notes
paragraphs: Use these prompts to produce a short record you can revisit. Date the sheet, identify the reference you used and leave unknowns explicitly unanswered. Keep site facts, personal preferences and requests for confirmation separate.
checklist: Which view carries the main idea?

sections.heading: What this exercise cannot establish
paragraphs: Transparency in a picture does not establish optical quality, weight or structural properties. A concept view is not a fabrication specification.

title: Choosing a visual priority in a crowded room
description: A crowded room brief needs a stated visual priority.

sections.heading: The question behind the worksheet
paragraphs: A crowded room brief needs a stated visual priority. Without one, every reference may compete to become the main feature.

sections.heading: Work through the observation
paragraphs: List the objects or areas you want people to notice, then rank only the first two. Describe why each matters. Test the proposed new object as a quieter companion and as a stronger focal element in separate sketches. Compare what each option asks the rest of the room to do.

sections.heading: A worked example to compare
paragraphs: A cherished wall piece may remain the priority while a table supports it through a simpler outline. Choosing that relationship avoids asking both to dominate the same view.

sections.heading: Questions to put in your notes
paragraphs: Use these prompts to produce a short record you can revisit. Date the sheet, identify the reference you used and leave unknowns explicitly unanswered. Keep site facts, personal preferences and requests for confirmation separate.
checklist: Which competing feature can become quieter?

sections.heading: What this exercise cannot establish
paragraphs: A priority is a preference for discussion, not a rule about taste. Other users may need a different practical arrangement.

paragraphs: Keep the resulting note with your current brief. Before sending it, check that it explains one decision clearly and does not turn a preference into an agreed detail. Use the current linked page for the relevant website guidance, and bring any piece-specific uncertainty to the atelier.

title: A scale study using paper outlines
description: Paper outlines make early scale discussions tangible without pretending to be finished prototypes.

sections.heading: The question behind the worksheet
paragraphs: Paper outlines make early scale discussions tangible without pretending to be finished prototypes. Their value is in the questions they reveal.

sections.heading: Work through the observation
paragraphs: Draw or cut an approximate outline and label its scale and assumptions. Place it on a room plan or use a safely positioned paper marker in an unobstructed area. Compare two options using the same reference edge. Record the difference in words as well as dimensions.

sections.heading: A worked example to compare
paragraphs: A longer outline may align with a wall feature but occupy more of a circulation area. The comparison can identify the next measurement to verify.

sections.heading: Questions to put in your notes
paragraphs: Use these prompts to produce a short record you can revisit. Date the sheet, identify the reference you used and leave unknowns explicitly unanswered. Keep site facts, personal preferences and requests for confirmation separate.
checklist: Which option needs a more accurate check?

sections.heading: What this exercise cannot establish
paragraphs: Paper does not represent height, weight, stability or actual handling. Avoid leaving markers where they could create a trip hazard.

paragraphs: Keep the resulting note with your current brief. Before sending it, check that it explains one decision clearly and does not turn a preference into an agreed detail. Use the current linked page for the relevant website guidance, and bring any piece-specific uncertainty to the atelier.
